ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a race track has a "pear-shaped" design. The two curved sections are a large circular arc with a radius of $R = 90\mathrm{m}$ and a small circular arc with a radius of $r = 40\mathrm{m}$. The straight sections are tangent to the curved sections. The distance between the centers $O$ and $O'$ of the large and small circular arcs is $L = 100\mathrm{m}$. When the race car travels along the curved track, the maximum static friction force between the road and the tires is 2.25 times the car's weight. Assume that the engine power is sufficiently large, the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, and the results can retain $\pi$ and square roots.

1. Determine the maximum speed at which the race car can maintain uniform circular motion on the small circular arc without skidding.
2. If the race car undergoes uniform acceleration in a straight line from the small circular arc to the large circular arc, and uniform deceleration in a straight line from the large circular arc to the small circular arc, while maintaining the maximum allowable speed for uniform circular motion on the curved sections, in order to minimize the lap time: a: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the race car during acceleration on the straight sections. b: Calculate the minimum lap time.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the figure: In the figure, the track is pear-shaped; the left side is a smaller circular arc segment, the center is labeled O', and the radius is labeled r; the right side is a larger circular arc segment, the center is labeled O, and the radius is labeled R. The two circular arc segments are connected by two upper and lower oblique straight lines, and the straight lines are tangent to the circular arcs. In the figure, O' and O are connected with a dashed line, and the distance is labeled L; a dashed radius is also drawn from O to the tangency point of the large circular arc, indicating that the radius is perpendicular to the tangent. Then reason: On the curve, the maximum static friction force provides the centripetal force, so mv^2/ρ ≤ 2.25mg, that is v_max = sqrt(2.25gρ). The small circular arc radius r=40 m, so v_small = sqrt(2.25×10×40)=sqrt(900)=30 m/s. The large circular arc radius R=90 m, so v_large = sqrt(2.25×10×90)=sqrt(2025)=45 m/s. Geometric relation: The two circular arcs are connected by two symmetric common external tangents, the distance between centers L=100 m, and the radius difference R-r=90-40=50 m. Let the angle related to the common tangent be θ, then sinθ=(R-r)/L=50/100=1/2, so θ=π/6. The length of each straight-line segment is d=Lcosθ=100×cos(π/6)=50√3 m. Because the radius is perpendicular to the tangent, the central angle corresponding to the small circular arc is π-2θ=π-π/3=2π/3, and the central angle corresponding to the large circular arc is π+2θ=π+π/3=4π/3. Therefore the small circular arc length s_small=r·2π/3=40·2π/3=80π/3 m; the large circular arc length s_large=R·4π/3=90·4π/3=120π m. The straight-line acceleration segment accelerates uniformly from 30 m/s to 45 m/s, with distance d=50√3 m. From v^2-v0^2=2ad, obtain: 45^2-30^2=2a·50√3, so a=1125/(100√3)=15√3/4 m/s^2. The magnitude of the acceleration in the deceleration segment is the same. The total time is the sum of the uniform-speed times on the two circular arcs and the variable-speed times on the two straight lines: small circular arc time t_small=(80π/3)/30=8π/9 s; large circular arc time t_large=120π/45=8π/3 s; total time on the two straight-line segments t_straight=2(45-30)/a=30/(15√3/4)=8√3/3 s. So the shortest lap time t=8π/9+8π/3+8√3/3=32π/9+8√3/3=(32π+24√3)/9 s.
